stem: How is billing calculated for shared pay-as-you-go inference requests versus dedicated endpoints?

options.text: Shared pay-as-you-go is billed by raw storage GBs; dedicated is billed per SQL query
options.explanation: Storage GBs belong to database/file storage billing, not LLM token inference billing.

options.text: Shared pay-as-you-go is billed per processed input/output token; dedicated is billed per provisioned GPU node hour
options.explanation: Shared models bill per 1M processed tokens, while dedicated instances bill fixed hourly rates for allocated node capacity.

options.text: Shared pay-as-you-go is free; dedicated charges a fixed annual license fee
options.explanation: Shared API usage incurs token consumption costs; dedicated endpoints charge per node hour.

options.text: Both charge identical flat fees per HTTP request regardless of length or hardware
options.explanation: Shared models bill dynamically on token length; dedicated endpoints bill per hardware instance hour.

stem: What cost control safeguard prevents unexpected usage charges on an organization account?

options.text: Disabling SSL certificate validation on requests
options.explanation: Disabling SSL compromises transport security and has no impact on billing thresholds.

options.text: Setting temperature to 1.0 on all completion calls
options.explanation: Temperature controls output entropy, not monetary spend caps.

options.text: Configuring spending budget alerts and hard credit caps on the organization account
options.explanation: Budget thresholds and hard spending caps prevent unexpected cost overruns.

options.text: Changing API request content-type to application/xml
options.explanation: MIME headers specify payload format, not billing caps.

stem: When configuring streaming responses in the Chat Completions API, what format are the event stream data chunks delivered in?

options.text: Server-Sent Events (SSE) data streams formatted with data: [JSON]
options.explanation: Streaming chat completions use standard Server-Sent Events (SSE) where each chunk is prefixed with data.

options.text: Raw binary WebSocket frame packets
options.explanation: The Chat Completions API uses standard HTTP streaming with SSE, not WebSockets.

options.text: A multipart/form-data MIME payload
options.explanation: Multipart encoding is used for file uploads, not streaming LLM tokens.

options.text: A single chunked JSON array containing all tokens
options.explanation: JSON arrays cannot be incrementally parsed per token without custom stream parsers; SSE line streams are used.

stem: How does setting temperature to 0.0 affect the sampling output of a chat completion model?

options.text: It causes the model to sample tokens purely randomly across the full vocabulary
options.explanation: High temperature increases randomness; zero temperature removes random sampling.

options.text: It enables deterministic greedy decoding by always selecting the highest-probability token
options.explanation: Setting temperature to 0 selects top logprob tokens deterministically (greedy decoding).

options.text: It disables system prompt instructions and safety filtering
options.explanation: Temperature only controls logit scaling during generation, not prompt handling or moderation.

options.text: It restricts token generation to a maximum of 100 completion tokens
options.explanation: Output length is controlled by max_tokens, not temperature.

stem: Two teams run separate GPU clusters that were placed in the same InfiniBand fabric. A security review asks whether one cluster's nodes could reach the other's over InfiniBand. What is the answer?

options.text: Yes, because sharing a fabric means sharing one InfiniBand address space
options.explanation: Sharing a fabric is exactly the case the partition key mechanism exists to handle, so a shared fabric does not imply reachability.

options.text: No, because each cluster gets a unique partition key that isolates its traffic
options.explanation: Correct. Per-cluster P-Keys isolate traffic inside a shared physical fabric, so this isolation holds without giving each cluster its own hardware.

options.text: Yes, unless a security group is attached to each node's network interface
options.explanation: Security groups filter VPC traffic on network interfaces; the InfiniBand fabric is a separate network whose isolation is not configured that way.

options.text: No, because two clusters can never be created in the same fabric
options.explanation: Multiple clusters do share a fabric — that is the normal arrangement, and why an isolation mechanism is needed at all.

stem: A training job on a GPU cluster is bottlenecked moving tensors between GPUs on different nodes. Which property of the cluster's networking is intended to address this?

options.text: Each node's traffic is serialized through a single shared host NIC
options.explanation: Serializing through one shared NIC would create a bottleneck rather than relieve one; each GPU has its own NIC.

options.text: Transfers are staged through object storage to decouple the endpoints
options.explanation: Staging through object storage adds a slower hop; it is not the mechanism that accelerates GPU-to-GPU exchange.

options.text: Data moves directly between each GPU and its NIC without passing through the CPU
options.explanation: Correct. GPUDirect RDMA takes the CPU out of the transfer path, which is what raises data exchange speed for this pattern.

options.text: The CPU copies each buffer into host memory before the NIC transmits it
options.explanation: That host-memory bounce is precisely the step the technology removes.

stem: You are creating a GPU cluster and must pick an InfiniBand fabric. Why does the choice constrain the cluster later?

options.text: The fabric fixes how many nodes the cluster may ever contain
options.explanation: Fabric capacity is finite, but the documented consequence of the choice is which GPU platform can be added, not a fixed node count.

options.text: The fabric determines which project the cluster's resources belong to
options.explanation: Project membership is an IAM concern and is unrelated to the physical fabric a cluster sits in.

options.text: The fabric sets the partition key that other tenants use to reach the cluster
options.explanation: A partition key isolates a cluster rather than granting anyone access, and it is assigned per cluster.

options.text: The fabric limits which GPU platform can be added to that cluster
options.explanation: Correct. Each fabric serves particular GPU platforms, so the fabric must be chosen against the GPU type you intend to run.

stem: A colleague creating their first Managed Service for Kubernetes cluster asks what leaving the public endpoint enabled will mean in practice. What should you tell them?

options.text: The cluster becomes reachable from the internet, so they can connect from any machine
options.explanation: Correct. That is what the public endpoint provides, and it is why the quickstart path can connect with kubectl from anywhere.

options.text: The cluster's nodes are moved onto public IP addresses in the default subnet
options.explanation: The endpoint concerns how the control plane is reached; the cluster's control plane and nodes still use private addresses from the subnet.

options.text: Every workload scheduled on the cluster is exposed on the internet automatically
options.explanation: Exposing workloads is done per service; enabling the cluster endpoint does not publish what runs inside.

options.text: The cluster can only be reached from inside the same node group
options.explanation: That describes no available option, and it is the opposite of what a public endpoint does.

stem: A VM was created in the wrong subnet. The team wants it moved to the correct subnet without rebuilding it. What is the outcome?

options.text: It can be moved once the VM is stopped, then restarted in the new subnet
options.explanation: Stopping the VM does not unlock the change; the assignment is fixed at creation regardless of power state.

options.text: It cannot be moved; the VM has to be recreated in the correct subnet
options.explanation: Correct. Network and subnet are set at creation and cannot be changed afterwards, so recreating the resource is the only route.

options.text: It can be moved by attaching a second network interface in the target subnet
options.explanation: Adding an interface does not relocate the resource, and the documented rule admits no such workaround.

options.text: It can be moved by editing the security group assigned to its interface
options.explanation: Security groups filter traffic; they do not determine which subnet a resource lives in.

stem: A team wants two test environments that use identical private IP addressing and must not be able to reach each other. What arrangement achieves this?

options.text: Put both in one network and rely on distinct subnet CIDR ranges
options.explanation: One network gives direct private connectivity between resources, and duplicate addressing is not possible within it.

options.text: Put both in one network and deny all traffic with security rules
options.explanation: Rules could block traffic, but they cannot let the same private IP address be assigned to resources in both environments.

options.text: Create a separate network for each environment
options.explanation: Correct. Separate networks are the documented answer both for disabling connectivity and for reusing the same private addresses.

options.text: Create one network per region and place the environments in different regions
options.explanation: Region placement is not what governs private connectivity or address reuse here.

stem: An engineer created a security group with the intended rules, but the VM's traffic is still unfiltered. What step is most likely missing?

options.text: The security group has not been associated with the VM's project
options.explanation: Security groups are associated with a network, and project membership is not what puts a group into effect for a VM.

options.text: The rules were created without a priority, so none of them are evaluated
options.explanation: Priority orders rules against one another; a missing association explains traffic being unfiltered altogether.

options.text: The VM must be restarted before any security group takes effect
options.explanation: A restart is not the documented requirement for a security group to apply.

options.text: The security group has not been assigned to the VM's network interface
options.explanation: Correct. A security group only applies to a VM once it is assigned to that VM's network interface.

stem: Two security rules in one group match the same packet with conflicting access settings. One has priority 1 and the other priority 900. Which wins?

options.text: The rule with priority 900, because larger values are evaluated first
options.explanation: The scale runs the other way: a larger number means lower priority.

options.text: The rule with priority 1, because 1 is the highest priority
options.explanation: Correct. Priority 1 is the highest and 1000 the lowest, so the lower number takes precedence.

options.text: Neither, because conflicting rules cause the group to be rejected
options.explanation: Conflicts are resolved by priority rather than by refusing the configuration.

options.text: Whichever rule is stateful, regardless of the priority values
options.explanation: Stateful versus stateless controls connection tracking, not which of two matching rules is applied.

stem: A workload writes intermediate shards to a local SSD disk. The VM is stopped overnight to save cost. What happens to that data?

options.text: It is erased, because local SSD disks are ephemeral
options.explanation: Correct. Local SSD data is erased when the VM is stopped or deleted, which is why it suits only recreatable data.

options.text: It is preserved, because the disk is physically attached to the host
options.explanation: Physical attachment is what makes the storage fast and host-local; it does not make it durable across a stop.

options.text: It is preserved only if the disk was created from a disk snapshot
options.explanation: Local SSD disks are not created as separate managed resources from images or snapshots.

options.text: It is migrated automatically to a network SSD disk on shutdown
options.explanation: No such migration happens; nothing moves the data off the host.

stem: Four running VMs must read and write one common dataset at the same time. Which storage option supports this directly?

options.text: One network SSD disk attached to all four VMs
options.explanation: A network SSD disk can only be added to one running VM at a time, so it cannot serve four simultaneously.

options.text: A local SSD disk on each VM holding its own copy
options.explanation: Per-VM copies are not one common dataset, and local SSD data does not survive a stop.

options.text: A boot disk image shared between the four VMs
options.explanation: Images are a source for creating boot disks, not a medium several VMs read and write concurrently.

options.text: A shared filesystem attached to all four VMs
options.explanation: Correct. A shared filesystem is file storage that can be attached to multiple VMs at once.

stem: An engineer tries to create a 100 GiB Network SSD Non-replicated disk and the request is rejected. What explains this?

options.text: Non-replicated disks have a fixed size that cannot be chosen
options.explanation: The size is chosen; it is the permitted increment that is constrained.

options.text: The size must be a multiple of 93 GiB, and 100 GiB is not
options.explanation: Correct. Data blocks sit in 93 GiB NVMe namespaces, so the disk size has to be a multiple of that.

options.text: Non-replicated disks cannot be used as additional disks
options.explanation: Their suitability is about redundancy, not about the additional-disk role.

options.text: Disks under 128 GiB must be local SSD disks
options.explanation: No such threshold governs the choice between the two kinds of disk.

stem: Two teams keep their VMs in separate projects in the same region and want both to mount one shared filesystem. What should you tell them?

options.text: It works if both projects belong to the same tenant
options.explanation: Sharing a tenant does not lift the restriction; the boundary that matters here is the project.

options.text: It works once the filesystem is mounted as a virtiofs device on each VM
options.explanation: Mounting as virtiofs is required on any VM the filesystem is attached to, but it does not permit crossing projects.

options.text: It is not supported; all attached VMs must be in the same project
options.explanation: Correct. Cross-project sharing is explicitly unsupported, even when the projects sit in the same region.

options.text: It works only if encryption is disabled on the filesystem
options.explanation: Filesystem encryption is on by default and cannot be disabled, and it has no bearing on project scope.

stem: A new engineer appears on the tenant user list but cannot see any resources. What is the most likely reason?

options.text: Their account has not finished federation sync and will populate shortly
options.explanation: Appearing on the user list already means the account exists; nothing further populates access on its own.

options.text: They need a service account key before resources become visible
options.explanation: Service account keys authenticate service accounts, not a human user browsing resources.

options.text: Resources are only visible to the user who created them
options.explanation: Visibility follows group membership rather than who created a resource.

options.text: They have not been assigned to a group, so no access has been granted
options.explanation: Correct. Being on the tenant user list grants nothing by itself; access comes from the group an account is assigned to.

stem: A service account was created in the tooling project. It now needs to manage buckets that live in a different project in the same tenant. Is that possible?

options.text: Yes, its access follows the groups it is added to, not the project it was created in
options.explanation: Correct. The creating project sets where the account lives, while group membership can extend its access anywhere in the tenant.

options.text: No, a service account can only ever act inside the project that created it
options.explanation: That is the intuition the documentation explicitly corrects; the account is not confined to its home project.

options.text: No, it must be recreated in the target project for each additional project
options.explanation: Recreating per project is unnecessary given how group membership determines access.

options.text: Yes, but only after the two projects are merged into one
options.explanation: Projects are not merged to share access, and nothing requires it here.

stem: An on-call rotation must be able to stop and start VMs during incidents, but should not gain broader Compute permissions. Which role fits?

options.text: `editor`, scoped to the project containing the VMs
options.explanation: The editor role grants management of most resource types, which is broader than the task requires.

options.text: `compute.instance-power-operator`
options.explanation: Correct. It exists precisely to allow power operations on VMs without broader Compute permissions.

options.text: `compute.serial-console-user`
options.explanation: That role covers interactive troubleshooting over the serial console, not powering machines on and off.

options.text: `viewer`, which permits state changes on resources it can see
options.explanation: The viewer role is for viewing resources and accessing data in them, not for changing their power state.

stem: A data-collection agent must drop files into a bucket but must not be able to read back or enumerate what is already there. Which role matches?

options.text: `storage.object-viewer`
options.explanation: That grants reading objects, which is what this agent must not be able to do.

options.text: `storage.object-lister`
options.explanation: Listing objects and viewing version metadata is exactly the enumeration being withheld.

options.text: `storage.uploader`
options.explanation: Correct. It allows viewing buckets and uploading objects while withholding listing and downloading.

options.text: `storage.editor`
options.explanation: That is a broad Object Storage role and grants far more than write-only submission.

stem: A project was created in the wrong region. What can be changed on it afterwards?

options.text: Its region, by editing the project and selecting another one
options.explanation: Region is fixed once the project exists.

options.text: Its tenant, by transferring the project to another tenant
options.explanation: A project cannot be moved to another tenant.

options.text: Both its region and tenant, provided the project holds no resources
options.explanation: Being empty does not unlock either change.

options.text: Only its name; the project must be recreated in the correct region
options.explanation: Correct. Name is the only editable field, so a wrong region means creating a new project.

stem: During a cleanup, a team asks you to delete an unused tenant along with its projects. What is the correct response?

options.text: Delete it after all its projects have been deleted first
options.explanation: Emptying the tenant does not make it deletable.

options.text: Tenants cannot be deleted, so the cleanup must stop at its contents
options.explanation: Correct. A tenant cannot be deleted; only what it contains can be cleaned up.

options.text: Delete it only if it was created after sign-up rather than automatically
options.explanation: How the tenant came to exist does not change whether it can be removed.

options.text: Delete it by removing every user account from it
options.explanation: Removing accounts changes who can act in the tenant, not whether the tenant exists.

stem: An automation script uses the Nebius AI Cloud CLI to create a project in a private region and fails. What is the explanation?

options.text: Project creation via the CLI is restricted to public regions
options.explanation: Correct. Attempting to create a project in a private region through the CLI returns an error.

options.text: Projects can only be created in the web console, never via the CLI
options.explanation: The CLI is a supported way to create projects; the constraint is which regions it covers.

options.text: A project already exists in that region, and only one is permitted
options.explanation: A project per region is created by default, but that does not cap the total at one.

options.text: Private regions require the project to be created without a name
options.explanation: No such requirement exists.

stem: Your organization's IdP has rotated the signing certificate used for single sign-on. What does the federation configuration in Nebius AI Cloud let you do about it?

options.text: Nothing; the federation must be deleted and created again
options.explanation: Certificates are managed on an existing federation, so a rebuild is not required.

options.text: Only deactivate the federation until the IdP is rolled back
options.explanation: Deactivation is available, but it is not the mechanism for handling a rotated certificate.

options.text: Rotate it automatically, since certificates are synced from the IdP
options.explanation: Certificates are uploaded and managed deliberately rather than synchronized on their own.

options.text: Upload the new certificate and delete the old one on the existing federation
options.explanation: Correct. Attached certificates can be uploaded or deleted as part of managing a federation.

stem: An engineer with the `editor` role is asked to set up a federation so staff can sign in through the company IdP. What blocks them?

options.text: Federations can only be created by the account that first signed up for the tenant
options.explanation: Access is governed by group membership rather than by who originally created the tenant.

options.text: Managing federations requires the `admin` role, which `editor` does not confer
options.explanation: Correct. The task requires being in a group holding the admin role at tenant or project scope.

options.text: Nothing blocks them; `editor` covers all identity configuration
options.explanation: The editor role manages most resource types, but identity federation is reserved for admins.

options.text: They must first be removed from every other group in the tenant
options.explanation: Group membership is additive; nothing requires stripping other memberships.

stem: You are preparing to create a federation and want to gather everything needed beforehand. What must you obtain from the identity provider?

options.text: A service account access key issued by the identity provider
options.explanation: Access keys authenticate service accounts against AWS-compatible APIs; they are unrelated to configuring an IdP.

options.text: The private signing key used by the identity provider
options.explanation: A private key is never handed over; the federation is configured with the public certificate instead.

options.text: The SAML application metadata: login URL, identifier and certificate
options.explanation: Correct. These are the values the federation is built from, obtained through the IdP admin portal.

options.text: A list of every user account that should be allowed to sign in
options.explanation: Users arrive through the federation itself; enumerating them up front is not part of creating it.

stem: A VM was created two minutes ago and its Metrics tab is empty. What is the appropriate response?

options.text: Reinstall the monitoring agent, since an empty tab means collection failed
options.explanation: Data is collected automatically; an empty tab this soon after creation is expected rather than a failure.

options.text: Raise a support case, because usage data should appear immediately
options.explanation: Immediate appearance is not what the platform promises, so there is nothing yet to escalate.

options.text: Widen the time filter, because the data is there but outside the window
options.explanation: Adjusting filters cannot surface data for a period in which none has been collected yet.

options.text: Wait, because usage data becomes available 5-10 minutes after the VM is created
options.explanation: Correct. There is a documented delay before a new VM's usage data appears.

stem: An engineer watching a dashboard during an incident asks how current the numbers are. What is true by default?

options.text: The data refreshes every 15 seconds, and the interval can be changed
options.explanation: Correct. Fifteen seconds is the default refresh, configurable next to the time filters.

options.text: The data refreshes only when the page is reloaded manually
options.explanation: The dashboard refreshes on its own; a manual reload is not required.

options.text: The data refreshes every five minutes and the interval is fixed
options.explanation: Neither the interval nor its immutability matches the dashboard's behaviour.

options.text: The data refreshes once per hour, matching the metrics retention window
options.explanation: An hourly cadence would be useless during an incident and is not what is configured.

stem: A brief utilization spike keeps paging the team. Which alert setting is intended to stop momentary spikes from firing?

options.text: Threshold, by raising the value the metric must reach
options.explanation: Raising the threshold changes what counts as a spike, but a brief excursion above the new value would still fire.

options.text: Duration, the time during which the condition must be met
options.explanation: Correct. Requiring the condition to hold for a period is what filters out momentary spikes.

options.text: Condition, by switching from exceeds to drops below
options.explanation: That inverts which direction triggers the alert rather than requiring persistence.

options.text: Metric, by selecting a different series to watch
options.explanation: Changing the series avoids this particular signal instead of handling its brevity.

stem: While adding a notification email to an alert, an engineer without admin rights sees a much shorter list of contacts than a colleague does. Why?

options.text: The list only shows emails that have never been used for notifications
options.explanation: The list is drawn from emails already used for notifications, not from unused ones.

options.text: The list is limited to contacts in the same project as the alert
options.explanation: Visibility follows admin rights rather than the project the alert belongs to.

options.text: Without admin rights, only their own contacts are visible
options.explanation: Correct. Admins see all tenant contacts; everyone else sees only their own.

options.text: The list hides anyone already subscribed to that same alert
options.explanation: Existing subscribers are not filtered out of the list.

stem: A node has been reporting the `NodeReady` condition as `False` for eight minutes. What does Managed Kubernetes do?

options.text: Nothing automatic; the node stays until an operator intervenes
options.explanation: Automatic recovery exists precisely so an operator does not have to act on this.

options.text: It reboots the node in place and keeps its name
options.explanation: The response to a false status is replacement rather than an in-place reboot.

options.text: It waits for the full 15-minute window that applies to any unhealthy node
options.explanation: Fifteen minutes is the threshold for the `Unknown` status; `False` is acted on after five.

options.text: It runs an automatic recovery, having passed the five-minute threshold
options.explanation: Correct. A `False` status lasting more than five minutes triggers automatic recovery.

stem: After a Network SSD NRD boot disk reported persistent I/O errors, the node disappeared and a differently named node appeared. What happened?

options.text: The node was renamed as part of resetting its boot disk
options.explanation: Nodes are not renamed in place; the new name belongs to a genuinely new node.

options.text: Automatic recovery deleted the node and created a new one with a healthy boot disk
options.explanation: Correct. That is the documented remedy for a boot disk with persistent I/O errors.

options.text: The autoscaler removed the node because its disk reduced available capacity
options.explanation: Scaling decisions are about capacity, not about a failing boot disk.

options.text: An operator must have drained and deleted it manually
options.explanation: No manual action is needed; the service performs this recovery itself.

stem: A team plans to scale a node group from six nodes to ten and worries the running workloads will be disrupted by node replacement. What should you tell them?

options.text: Scaling does not recreate nodes, so existing nodes are left in place
options.explanation: Correct. Scaling a node group up or down does not recreate any nodes; replacement comes from template changes instead.

options.text: Every node is replaced on any change to the node group's size
options.explanation: Replacement is triggered by modifying the node group template, not by changing its size.

options.text: Scaling always drains and recreates one node at a time
options.explanation: That describes the rolling update that follows a template change.

options.text: Scaling is only safe when the group is first cordoned entirely
options.explanation: No such precaution is required for scaling.

stem: A team stops several GPU VMs overnight and expects the freed quota to let them launch a new cluster. Does it?

options.text: Yes, stopped VMs release their quota until they are started again
options.explanation: Stopping does not release quota; the reservation persists while the VM exists.

options.text: Yes, but only for GPU quotas, not for storage quotas
options.explanation: The rule does not distinguish stopped from running for either category.

options.text: No, quota is only released once the region's capacity is rebalanced
options.explanation: Quota accounting is not tied to capacity rebalancing.

options.text: No, a VM counts toward quota from creation to deletion regardless of power state
options.explanation: Correct. Only deleting the VM releases what it counts against.

stem: A Managed Kubernetes node group fails to grow because of a quota limit, though no standalone VMs were created. Why is a Compute quota involved?

options.text: Node groups consume a separate Kubernetes quota that mirrors Compute limits
options.explanation: There is no mirrored quota; the nodes count against the Compute quotas themselves.

options.text: Managed Kubernetes nodes are based on Compute VMs and count against the same quotas
options.explanation: Correct. The quotas cover Compute VMs and equally the Kubernetes and Soperator nodes built on them.

options.text: The cluster's control plane counts as a virtual machine in the quota
options.explanation: The nodes are what consume the quota here, not the managed control plane.

options.text: Compute quota is only consulted when a node group uses a GPU cluster
options.explanation: The accounting does not depend on whether the node group is attached to a GPU cluster.

stem: Planning capacity, an engineer assumes one VM quota governs every machine type. What correction is needed?

options.text: Quotas are per project and identical across all machine types within it
options.explanation: Quotas do vary by scope, but the distinction being missed here is between GPU and non-GPU machines.

options.text: Quotas apply only to GPU virtual machines; other machines are unlimited
options.explanation: Non-GPU virtual machines are also subject to quotas.

options.text: Compute has different quotas for GPU and non-GPU virtual machines
options.explanation: Correct. The two categories are governed separately, so one number does not describe both.

options.text: Quotas apply to storage only, since compute is billed rather than capped
options.explanation: Compute has quotas on virtual machines as well as on storage and InfiniBand usage.

stem: PyTorch on a multi-GPU VM fails with `system not yet initialized (error 802)`. Which cause should you investigate first?

options.text: The GPU quota for the project has been exhausted
options.explanation: A quota problem prevents creating machines; it does not surface as a CUDA initialization error on a running VM.

options.text: The boot disk image lacks an NVIDIA driver
options.explanation: The error reports that the driver is present but CUDA failed to initialize.

options.text: A security group is blocking traffic between the GPUs
options.explanation: GPU initialization on a single VM does not depend on VPC traffic filtering.

options.text: The `nvidia-fabricmanager` service failed to initialize at VM startup
options.explanation: Correct. A race condition or timing issue can leave that service uninitialized, which breaks CUDA initialization.

stem: You have confirmed a CUDA initialization failure on a GPU VM. What is the documented range of remedies?

options.text: Restart the NVIDIA Fabric Manager service, the GPUs, or the entire VM
options.explanation: Correct. These are the three documented remedies, in increasing order of disruption.

options.text: Recreate the VM from a different boot disk image
options.explanation: The failure is not attributed to the image, and rebuilding is not the documented fix.

options.text: Detach and reattach the local SSD disks holding the workload data
options.explanation: Storage attachment is unrelated to CUDA initialization.

options.text: Move the VM into a different InfiniBand fabric
options.explanation: Fabric choice concerns cluster networking and cannot be changed for an existing resource anyway.

stem: A team believes CUDA initialization failures only affect one GPU platform, and plans to migrate away from it. Is that reasoning sound?

options.text: Yes, the failure is specific to eight-GPU platforms
options.explanation: The number of GPUs is explicitly not what determines exposure.

options.text: No, it can occur on any VM with GPUs regardless of platform, GPU count or image
options.explanation: Correct. The failure is not tied to a platform, so migrating on that basis would not remove it.

options.text: Yes, but only for VMs built from custom disk images
options.explanation: The boot disk image is explicitly not a differentiator.

options.text: No, because the failure only affects VMs inside GPU clusters
options.explanation: It is not confined to clustered VMs either.

stem: An intermittent VM fault has just cleared. Support asks for diagnostic logs. What is the best practice?

options.text: Collect them now that the system is stable, so the output is not distorted
options.explanation: A recovered system no longer holds the evidence that explains the fault.

options.text: Collect only the logs that postdate the recovery, to avoid noise
options.explanation: Excluding the broken period discards precisely what the investigation needs.

options.text: Collect logs while the issue is still occurring, because they capture more about the broken state
options.explanation: Correct. Logs taken during the fault carry more information than logs taken after it clears.

options.text: Collect no logs and reproduce the fault in a fresh VM instead
options.explanation: Reproduction may be impossible for an intermittent fault, and log collection is the documented first step.

stem: An engineer new to Logs asks how any LogQL query must begin. What is the answer?

options.text: With an aggregation function that defines the range
options.explanation: Aggregations may appear later in a query, but they are not how one begins.

options.explanation: The flavors differ in pricing, latency and optimization level, not in the answers produced.

options.text: No, both flavors deliver identical model outputs
options.explanation: Correct. The difference is in token pricing, latency and applied optimizations, not in what the model returns.

options.text: Yes, Fast truncates long responses to keep latency down
options.explanation: Nothing about the flavor shortens responses.

options.text: No, because Fast is only a billing label with no runtime difference
options.explanation: There is a real runtime difference: smaller batch sizes, more compute and techniques such as speculative decoding.

stem: An engineering team wants to understand what actually makes the Fast flavor faster. Which description matches?

options.text: It routes requests to a geographically closer region
options.explanation: Region choice is a dedicated endpoint concern, not what defines this flavor.

options.text: It reduces the model's parameter count to shorten computation
options.explanation: The model is unchanged; a smaller model would not deliver identical outputs.

options.text: It uses smaller batch sizes, more compute, and techniques such as speculative decoding
options.explanation: Correct. Those are the levers the Fast flavor pulls to reduce latency and improve responsiveness.

options.text: It caps the number of output tokens the model may generate
options.explanation: No output cap is part of the flavor.

stem: How does speculative decoding raise throughput without degrading output quality?

options.text: An auxiliary model pre-generates likely tokens that the main model then verifies
options.explanation: Correct. Verification by the main model is what preserves quality while cutting the number of forward passes.

options.text: Low-confidence tokens are dropped from the response before it is returned
options.explanation: Dropping tokens would change the output, which is exactly what this technique avoids.

options.text: The prompt is truncated so fewer tokens need to be processed
options.explanation: Truncating input is not part of the technique and would change results.

options.text: Several user requests are merged into a single forward pass
options.explanation: Batching multiple sequences together describes continuous batching instead.

stem: A stakeholder asks which optimization reduces memory usage by lowering the numeric precision of the model itself. Which one is it?

options.text: Paged Attention
options.explanation: That divides the input sequence into chunks processed separately, which is a memory layout change rather than a precision change.

options.text: Continuous Batching
options.explanation: That groups multiple input sequences to raise throughput; precision is untouched.

options.text: KV Cache
options.explanation: That stores frequently accessed key-value pairs to avoid recomputation.

options.text: Quantization
options.explanation: Correct. It reduces the precision of model weights and activations, lowering memory use and computation.

stem: A team plans an application that must read screenshots and answer questions about them. Which model type do they need?

options.text: Embedding
options.explanation: Embedding models turn inputs into vectors for search and similarity, not into answers about an image.

options.text: Vision
options.explanation: Correct. Vision is the supported modality for turning image input into text.

options.text: Text-to-text
options.explanation: Text-to-text covers generative language tasks and does not accept image input.

options.text: Any text-to-text model configured with a longer context window
options.explanation: Context length governs how much text fits, not whether images can be interpreted.

stem: Comparing two candidate models on their cards in the UI, a team wants a published measure of answer quality. Which field carries it?

options.text: Tokens per second, since faster models are better tuned
options.explanation: That is an approximate generation speed and says nothing about answer quality.

options.text: Input tokens, since richer models cost more per token
options.explanation: That is a price in USD per million tokens, not a quality measure.

options.text: Quality, which reports the MMLU score published by the model provider
options.explanation: Correct. The Quality field on the card is the provider-reported MMLU score.

options.text: Output tokens, which reflects how much reasoning the model produces
options.explanation: That is the price of generated tokens, again a cost rather than a quality signal.

stem: A finance stakeholder asks how per-token pricing is presented when comparing models in the UI. What should you tell them?

options.text: As a monthly subscription per model
options.explanation: Pricing shown on the card is per token, not a recurring subscription.

options.text: In USD per million tokens, separately for input and output
options.explanation: Correct. Input and output tokens are each priced in USD per million tokens.

options.text: As a single blended rate covering both input and output
options.explanation: The two directions are listed separately, precisely because they differ.

options.text: In USD per request, regardless of length
options.explanation: Charging is per token, so request length matters.

stem: A team starts a fine-tuning job and does not set `context_length`. What length applies?

options.text: The maximum the base model supports
options.explanation: The default is not the model's maximum; it must be raised deliberately.

options.text: 131072 tokens, the largest supported value
options.explanation: That is the top of the supported range, not the default.

options.text: No default; the job fails until the value is supplied
options.explanation: The job does not require the hyperparameter, because a default applies.

options.text: 8192 tokens
options.explanation: Correct. Unless overridden by the hyperparameter, fine-tuning defaults to 8192 tokens.

stem: When shortlisting a base model to fine-tune, which two properties does the supported-models reference let you compare?

options.text: Supported context lengths and available fine-tuning types
options.explanation: Correct. The page lists which context lengths a base model supports and whether LoRA, full fine-tuning, or both are available.

options.text: Training data sources and benchmark leaderboards
options.explanation: Neither is what this reference enumerates.

options.text: Guaranteed throughput and regional availability
options.explanation: Those concern serving capacity rather than fine-tuning support.

options.text: Hourly GPU price and reserved capacity terms
options.explanation: Pricing and reservations are billing topics, not properties of a base model.

stem: A team wants the full parameter list for every model programmatically, not just what the card shows. How do they get it?

options.text: Open each model card and copy the values by hand
options.explanation: That is the manual path the API query parameter exists to replace.

options.text: Request the List models endpoint with `verbose=true`
options.explanation: Correct. That query parameter returns the extended list of model parameters.

options.text: Export the setup as code from the playground
options.explanation: Exporting code reproduces one chat setup, not the catalogue of model parameters.

options.text: Enable comparison mode and read both panels
options.explanation: Comparison shows two setups side by side in the UI rather than returning data.

stem: A developer asks how to send traffic to the Fast flavor of a model from their application. What is required?

options.text: Set a flavor field in the request body
options.explanation: The flavor is selected through the model name rather than a separate field.

options.text: Call a different base URL reserved for Fast endpoints
options.explanation: The endpoint stays the same; only the model name changes.

options.text: Append `-fast` to the model name in the API
options.explanation: Correct. The suffix on the model name is what selects the Fast flavor.

options.text: Request access from support before the flavor becomes callable
options.explanation: Both flavors are available without a request; one is chosen per call.

stem: Which factors determine the inference performance of an endpoint?

options.text: Only the number of parameters in the chosen model
options.explanation: Model size matters, but the endpoint's configuration is what this list describes.

options.text: Only the region the caller sends requests from
options.explanation: Region affects latency for a dedicated deployment but is not this set of factors.

options.text: The length of the system prompt supplied by the application
options.explanation: Prompt length affects individual requests, not how the endpoint itself is configured.

options.text: Batch size, GPU type, GPU count, and inference-time optimizations
options.explanation: Correct. Performance follows from how the endpoint balances these four.

stem: Which optimization works by splitting an input sequence into smaller chunks that are processed separately?

options.text: Paged Attention
options.explanation: Correct. Chunking the input this way reduces memory usage and computation.

options.text: Context Caching
options.explanation: That stores the output of previous layers for each input sequence to avoid recomputation.

options.text: Flash Attention
options.explanation: That is a modified attention mechanism that reduces the computations attention requires.

options.text: Quantization
options.explanation: That lowers numeric precision rather than restructuring the sequence.

stem: An application repeatedly sends requests that share a long common prefix. Which optimization is described as storing the output of previous layers for each input sequence?

options.text: Continuous Batching
options.explanation: That batches multiple sequences together to reduce per-request overhead.

options.text: Speculative decoding
options.explanation: That predicts likely next tokens with an auxiliary model and verifies them.

options.text: Flash Attention
options.explanation: That reduces the computations needed for attention calculations.

options.text: Context Caching
options.explanation: Correct. It caches the context — the output of previous layers — for each input sequence, cutting recomputation.

stem: A non-technical product manager wants to try a model and shape its behaviour before any engineering work is scheduled. What should they use?

options.text: A dedicated endpoint deployed with minimum replicas set to one
options.explanation: Deploying an endpoint is an infrastructure step and is not needed to try a model.

options.text: The Playground, which requires no coding
options.explanation: Correct. It exists so a model can be exercised through a web interface without writing code.

options.text: A fine-tuning job on a small sample of data
options.explanation: Fine-tuning changes the model and is far heavier than trying one out.

options.text: The List models endpoint with `verbose=true`
options.explanation: That returns model parameters rather than letting someone interact with a model.

stem: In the Playground, which control is intended for the instructions that guide how the model behaves across a conversation?

options.text: The system prompt, where few-shot examples can also be added
options.explanation: Correct. It holds behavioural instructions, and few-shot examples there demonstrate the desired output format.

options.text: The prompt preset, which stores behaviour permanently for all users
options.explanation: A preset saves a setup for later use or sharing; it is not itself the instruction field.

options.text: The View code panel, which fixes behaviour in the exported snippet
options.explanation: That exports the current setup for use in an application.

options.text: The Compare view, which applies instructions to both chats at once
options.explanation: Compare runs two setups side by side; parameters and prompts are copied deliberately between them.

stem: A team is torn between two prompt-and-parameter configurations and wants a like-for-like trial. What does the Playground offer?

options.text: A batch evaluation that scores both against a labelled dataset
options.explanation: No scoring harness is described; the comparison is interactive.

options.text: An automatic winner based on the MMLU score of each setup
options.explanation: MMLU is a provider-reported figure on the model card, not a verdict on two setups.

options.text: Compare, which opens two chat windows fed the same input at once
options.explanation: Correct. Compare runs two setups side by side and can submit inputs to both simultaneously.

options.text: A rolling deployment that shifts traffic between the two
options.explanation: Traffic shifting is a deployment concern, not a Playground feature.

stem: An application must keep inference inside a particular jurisdiction. Which dedicated endpoint control addresses that?

options.text: Autoscaling, by keeping replicas within one pool
options.explanation: Autoscaling governs how capacity follows traffic, not where it runs.

options.text: Region, which is chosen to meet data residency requirements
options.explanation: Correct. Region selection is what optimizes latency and satisfies data residency.

options.text: GPU configuration, by selecting hardware sold in that market
options.explanation: GPU type and count are matched to performance needs rather than jurisdiction.

options.text: Lifecycle management, by stopping the endpoint outside business hours
options.explanation: Stopping and starting a deployment does not constrain where it runs.

stem: How is a dedicated endpoint deployment managed versus how inference traffic reaches it?

options.text: Both go through the control plane, with the data plane reserved for logs
options.explanation: Inference runs through the data plane, not the control plane.

options.text: Both go through the data plane, with the control plane used only for billing
options.explanation: Creating and managing deployments is exactly what the control plane is for.

options.text: The control plane creates and manages deployments; the data plane serves inference over OpenAI-compatible APIs
options.explanation: Correct. That split is what the overview describes.

options.text: Deployments are managed through the Playground, and traffic through the control plane
options.explanation: The Playground is for experimenting with models, not for managing deployments.

stem: A workload's traffic varies sharply between business hours and overnight. Which dedicated endpoint control is designed for that?

options.text: Region, by placing the deployment near the daytime user base
options.explanation: Region placement addresses latency and residency, not fluctuating demand.

options.text: Lifecycle management, by deleting and recreating the deployment daily
options.explanation: Lifecycle operations exist, but they are not the mechanism for tracking traffic automatically.

options.text: GPU configuration, by choosing a GPU type that idles cheaply
options.explanation: GPU selection sets performance per replica rather than adjusting capacity over time.

options.text: Autoscaling, by setting minimum and maximum replicas
options.explanation: Correct. Minimum and maximum replicas let capacity scale with traffic automatically.

stem: After settling on a prompt and parameters in the Playground, a team wants the same setup available to colleagues later. What does the tool provide?

options.text: Saving the setup as a prompt preset for later use or sharing
options.explanation: Correct. A preset stores the configuration so it can be reused or shared.

options.text: Publishing the setup as a dedicated endpoint
options.explanation: Deploying an endpoint is an infrastructure action, not how a Playground setup is retained.

options.text: Committing the setup to the model card
options.explanation: Model cards report the model's own parameters and pricing; they are not per-team storage.

options.text: Nothing; the setup must be rebuilt each session
options.explanation: Setups can be both exported as code and saved as presets.

stem: A developer has finished tuning a chat setup in the Playground and needs it inside their application. What is the intended path?

options.text: Re-enter the parameters by hand in the application code
options.explanation: Manual transcription is what the export feature exists to avoid.

options.text: Export it as code with View code, which includes the chat
options.explanation: Correct. View code copies the model setup, chat included, for use in an application.

options.text: Grant the application access to the saved preset at runtime
options.explanation: Presets store a setup for people to reuse in the UI, not as a runtime API.

options.text: Fine-tune a model so the behaviour is baked into the weights
options.explanation: Fine-tuning is a far heavier step and is not how a prompt setup moves into code.

stem: Leadership asks what dedicated endpoints give the business that shared inference does not. Which pair of use cases is documented?

options.text: Free trial capacity and unlimited request rates
options.explanation: Neither is offered; trial credit and rate limits are separate topics with their own rules.

options.text: Automatic prompt optimization and managed evaluation
options.explanation: No such capabilities are attributed to dedicated endpoints.

options.text: Zero-cost idling and permanent GPU reservation
options.explanation: Capacity is released when an endpoint stops, and billing follows running replicas.

options.text: Predictable capacity and serving a finetuned base model with custom weights
options.explanation: Correct. Those are the documented key use cases for dedicated endpoints.

stem: An architect asks how much control a dedicated endpoint gives over the hardware behind a deployment. What is accurate?

options.text: GPU type and the number of GPUs per replica are both selectable
options.explanation: Correct. Both are chosen to match the deployment's performance and throughput needs.

options.text: Only the total number of replicas can be chosen; hardware is assigned
options.explanation: GPU type and GPUs per replica are explicitly under the customer's control.

options.text: Hardware is fixed per region and cannot be influenced
options.explanation: Region is a separate control from GPU configuration.

options.text: GPU type is selectable only under an enterprise contract
options.explanation: Selecting GPU type is part of configuring a dedicated endpoint.

stem: A downstream service needs the model's answer in a fixed shape it can parse. What does the platform provide by default, and what must change?

options.text: Output is JSON by default; a parameter switches it to prose
options.explanation: The default is natural language, not JSON.

options.text: Output is natural language by default; `response_format` forces JSON
options.explanation: Correct. Text is the default, and the parameter is what makes the response machine-readable.

options.text: Output shape is set per model and cannot be changed per request
options.explanation: The shape is chosen per request through the parameter.

options.text: Output must be reshaped by a second model after generation
options.explanation: A second pass is unnecessary when the format can be requested directly.

stem: A team sets `response_format` to `{"type": "json_object"}` and is surprised the field names vary between calls. Why?

options.text: The setting only applies to the first message in a conversation
options.explanation: Nothing limits the parameter to the opening message.

options.text: Field names always vary unless the temperature is set to zero
options.explanation: Sampling settings do not determine whether a schema is enforced.

options.text: That setting forces arbitrary JSON and lets the model decide the schema
options.explanation: Correct. `json_object` guarantees JSON but not any particular shape; the model chooses it.

options.text: The setting was ignored because a schema was not also supplied
options.explanation: It is not ignored; it produces valid JSON of the model's own design.

stem: Which `response_format` setting should be used when the response must conform to a schema the application supplies?

options.text: `{"type": "json_object"}`, with the schema described in the system prompt
options.explanation: That yields arbitrary JSON; a prompt alone does not bind the response to the schema.

options.text: `{"type": "text"}`, with a post-processing validation step
options.explanation: That returns natural language and pushes all the work downstream.

options.text: No setting is needed; schemas are inferred from the request body
options.explanation: Nothing infers a schema automatically.

options.text: `{"type": "json_schema"}`, supplying the schema in the request
options.explanation: Correct. That is the setting that makes the response follow a schema you provide.

stem: A team already passes a JSON schema in the request. What additional practice does the documentation recommend?

options.text: Also describe the schema in the text prompt given to the model
options.explanation: Correct. Practical testing showed it is always better to supply the schema in both places.

options.text: Send the schema only in the prompt and drop the parameter
options.explanation: Dropping the parameter would remove the mechanism that enforces the shape.

options.text: Split the schema across several requests to stay within limits
options.explanation: No such splitting is suggested.

options.text: Validate the schema by first requesting an arbitrary JSON object
options.explanation: A preliminary arbitrary-JSON call is not part of the recommendation.

stem: A model returns a tool call for a function your application defined. Who runs the function?

options.text: The inference platform, which proxies the call to the named service
options.explanation: The platform emits instructions; it does not reach out to external services on your behalf.

options.text: Your application, which executes it and feeds the result back
options.explanation: Correct. The model does not execute functions; parsing the output and running the code is your responsibility.

options.text: The model, once the tool schema has been registered
options.explanation: Registering a schema tells the model how a tool is invoked, not that the model runs it.

options.text: Whichever MCP server is connected to the conversation
options.explanation: MCP servers are one thing tools can reach, but execution is still driven by your code.

stem: How is each available tool described to the model?

options.text: As a natural-language sentence in the system prompt
options.explanation: Prompt text can add guidance, but tools are declared structurally.

options.text: As an example request and response pair
options.explanation: Examples may help behaviour, but they are not the tool definition.

options.text: As a JSON Schema giving its name, input parameters and data types
options.explanation: Correct. That schema is what tells the model how the tool should be invoked.

options.text: As a URL the model calls directly when needed
options.explanation: The model proposes calls rather than invoking endpoints itself.

stem: A product manager asks what function calling makes possible that a bare text model cannot do. Which capability is documented?

options.text: Retrieving real-time data through external code or services
options.explanation: Correct. Reaching live data and third-party services is exactly what tool integration enables.

options.text: Increasing the model's context window beyond its published limit
options.explanation: Context length is a property of the model, unchanged by tool use.

options.text: Guaranteeing the response is valid JSON
options.explanation: That is what structured output settings are for.

options.text: Removing per-token charges for tool responses
options.explanation: Tool use does not alter how tokens are billed.

stem: Given a user query and a set of available tools, what are the model's two documented options?

options.text: Execute a tool, or escalate the request to a human reviewer
options.explanation: The model never executes tools, and no human escalation path is described.

options.text: Respond conversationally, or propose a function call with filled-in arguments
options.explanation: Correct. It analyses intent and either answers directly or suggests a call matching the schema.

options.text: Return JSON, or return natural language, depending on the tool schema
options.explanation: Output format is governed by response_format, not by tool availability.

options.text: Call every registered tool, then summarize the combined results
options.explanation: Tools are selected by relevance rather than invoked exhaustively.

stem: A team stops a dedicated endpoint overnight to save money and expects the same GPUs back in the morning. What actually happens?

options.text: The GPUs are held for the endpoint and reattached on start
options.explanation: Nothing holds the previous GPUs; there is no such mechanism.

options.text: The GPUs are held only if the endpoint was stopped manually
options.explanation: The release happens regardless of why the endpoint stopped.

options.text: Capacity returns to a shared pool and is requested anew on start
options.explanation: Correct. Capacity is allocated only while the endpoint runs, and a restart re-requests it subject to availability.

options.text: The endpoint keeps its minimum replicas reserved while stopped
options.explanation: The minimum replicas guarantee applies only while the endpoint is running.

stem: A business continuity plan assumes a dedicated endpoint will return to full capacity immediately after a maintenance window. What risk should you flag?

options.text: Restarting may take longer than the first deployment when capacity is scarce
options.explanation: Correct. Under high demand or for scarce GPU types, capacity may be temporarily unavailable and the restart can take significantly longer.

options.text: The endpoint's model weights must be uploaded again after maintenance
options.explanation: Nothing indicates weights are lost across a maintenance event.

options.text: The endpoint is deleted automatically if maintenance exceeds an hour
options.explanation: Maintenance does not delete deployments.

options.text: Billing continues at full rate while the endpoint waits for capacity
options.explanation: Charges apply when replicas are running, so a stopped endpoint is not billed at full rate.

stem: An operations dashboard shows a dedicated endpoint as Updating. What does that indicate?

options.text: The endpoint is being created for the first time
options.explanation: That is the Starting stage.

options.text: The endpoint has failed and is retrying deployment
options.explanation: Updating describes configuration being applied, not a failure state.

options.text: The endpoint is applying configuration changes and capacity may degrade
options.explanation: Correct. Traffic may continue during an update while capacity temporarily degrades.

options.text: The endpoint's model is being replaced with a newer published version
options.explanation: Nothing swaps the model automatically under this status.

stem: Why do dedicated endpoints report two separate status types rather than one?

options.text: To distinguish billing state from technical state
options.explanation: Billing follows running replicas and is not one of the two status types.

options.text: To separate deployment progress from whether traffic can be served
options.explanation: Correct. Lifecycle describes the stage, readiness describes current ability to serve.

options.text: To report the control plane and the data plane independently
options.explanation: The planes describe how the endpoint is managed and used, not these statuses.

options.text: To track the minimum and maximum replica counts separately
options.explanation: Replica bounds are autoscaling settings rather than statuses.

stem: A finance lead asks when a dedicated endpoint incurs charges. What is the rule?

options.text: From creation until deletion, regardless of replica count
options.explanation: Charges track running replicas, not the mere existence of the endpoint.

options.text: Only while traffic is actively being served
options.explanation: A running replica is billable whether or not requests are arriving.

options.text: Whenever at least one replica is running
options.explanation: Correct. One or more running replicas makes the endpoint active, accessible and billable.

options.text: Monthly in advance, based on the maximum replica setting
options.explanation: Billing follows actual running replicas rather than a pre-purchased maximum.

stem: An endpoint has been scaled to zero replicas. What is the billing and availability position?

options.text: It remains billable so its capacity stays reserved
options.explanation: Capacity is not retained once released, and charges do not apply.

options.text: It is not accessible and no charges apply
options.explanation: Correct. With zero replicas running, the endpoint serves nothing and is not billed.

options.text: It is still accessible, served from a shared pool at a reduced rate
options.explanation: There is no reduced-rate shared serving mode for a scaled-to-zero endpoint.

options.text: It is billed at the minimum replica rate regardless
options.explanation: Minimum replicas are allocated only while the endpoint is active.

stem: What happens to an account when an automatic card charge fails?

options.text: The account is suspended
options.explanation: Correct. A failed charge suspends the account, which is why the payment method must stay valid.

options.text: Requests continue but are throttled to the free tier
options.explanation: No free-tier fallback is described.

options.text: The balance is carried to the next month with a fee
options.explanation: Nothing describes deferring the balance in this way.

options.text: Dedicated endpoints keep running while shared inference stops
options.explanation: The consequence applies to the account rather than to one product.

stem: Under which conditions is a bank card charged automatically?

options.text: Only when the customer manually tops up the balance
options.explanation: A manual top-up is an alternative to automatic charging, not a trigger for it.

options.text: Only at the end of a billing period, in arrears
options.explanation: The balance is debited in real time, with charges triggered by the conditions below.

options.text: At the start of the month if the balance is negative, or when the billing threshold is reached
options.explanation: Correct. Those are the two documented triggers, each charging enough to bring the balance back to zero.

options.text: Whenever any request is made against a paid model
options.explanation: Charging is not per request; the balance is debited and settled on those triggers.

stem: What response headers should client applications inspect to monitor remaining request and token quotas in real time?

options.text: x-server-ip and x-dns-host
options.explanation: Server IP and DNS host headers provide network routing metadata, not quota tracking.

options.text: content-type and content-length
options.explanation: Content-Type and Content-Length describe HTTP payload MIME type and byte size.

options.text: set-cookie and cache-control
options.explanation: Cookies and cache headers manage browser caching and session state.

options.text: x-ratelimit-remaining-requests and x-ratelimit-remaining-tokens
options.explanation: Response headers x-ratelimit-remaining-requests and x-ratelimit-remaining-tokens track real-time quota headroom.

stem: Which metric token usage counts are returned in standard Chat Completion response payloads under the usage object?

options.text: prompt_tokens, completion_tokens, and total_tokens
options.explanation: The usage object reports exact counts for prompt_tokens, completion_tokens, and total_tokens.

options.text: gpu_temperature_celsius and fan_speed_rpm
options.explanation: Hardware temperature and fan metrics belong to infrastructure monitoring, not model API usage payloads.

options.text: disk_write_mbps and network_latency_ms
options.explanation: Disk throughput and network ping latency are transport metrics, not LLM token usage counters.

options.text: database_connections_active
options.explanation: Database connections are SQL pool counters, not inference token usage object properties.

stem: Two teams must not see each other's datasets or endpoints. Which level of the resource model isolates them?

options.text: A project, since resources live inside it and inherit its access settings
options.explanation: Because resources take their access from the enclosing project, giving each team its own project is what produces the isolation.

options.text: The organization, since it is the top of the hierarchy
options.explanation: The organization is the shared container above projects, so placing both teams in one does not separate them.

options.text: The API key, since each key is scoped to a single resource
options.explanation: Keys are issued within a project. They express access, but the project is what bounds it.

options.text: An organization group, since groups own resources directly
options.explanation: Groups configure identity and access for people. Resources belong to projects, not to groups.

stem: What exists immediately after you sign up, before you create anything?

options.text: Nothing until you create an organization yourself
options.explanation: You can create further organizations later, but the first one is not something you have to set up.

options.text: A shared default organization common to all new users
options.explanation: The organization created at signup is yours, not a tenancy shared with strangers.

options.text: A project, with an organization created only when you invite someone
options.explanation: The hierarchy runs organization then project, so the organization cannot appear second.

options.text: A personal organization, created automatically
options.explanation: Signup provisions an organization for you, so there is always a workspace to create projects in.

stem: Which scope level in Nebius Token Factory directly owns API keys, budget limits, and deployed resources?

options.text: Projects
options.explanation: API keys, budgets, and endpoints belong to a specific Project within an Organization.

options.text: Global user profile
options.explanation: User profiles span across organizations but do not own resource quotas directly.

options.text: Region endpoints
options.explanation: Regions dictate data residency, not project isolation or credential scopes.

options.text: Model registry
options.explanation: The model registry is a global catalog of available base weights.

stem: What happens when a new user signs up for Nebius Token Factory for the first time?

options.text: A personal organization is created automatically for the user
options.explanation: First-time signup automatically provisions a personal organization.

options.text: The user must submit a support ticket to request organization creation
options.explanation: Organization provisioning is automated during account onboarding.

options.text: The user is assigned to a shared public sandbox organization
options.explanation: Each user gets an isolated personal organization, not a shared sandbox.

options.text: Access is restricted until an enterprise agreement is uploaded
options.explanation: Self-service signup creates a personal organization immediately.

stem: Latency matters more than token cost for your chat feature. How do you request the Fast flavor of a model?

options.text: Set a `flavor` parameter to `fast` in the request body

options.text: `json_schema` — the model chooses the schema itself
options.explanation: Schema-following mode is the opposite case: you supply the schema and the output conforms to it.
